==Problem==

How many ordered pairs <math>(a, b)</math> of positive integers satisfy the equation 
<cmath>a\cdot b + 63 = 20\cdot \text{lcm}(a, b) + 12\cdot\text{gcd}(a,b),</cmath>
where <math>\text{gcd}(a,b)</math> denotes the greatest common divisor of <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>, and <math>\text{lcm}(a,b)</math> denotes their least common multiple?

<math>\textbf{(A)} \text{ 0} \qquad \textbf{(B)} \text{ 2} \qquad \textbf{(C)} \text{ 4} \qquad \textbf{(D)} \text{ 6} \qquad \textbf{(E)} \text{ 8}</math>

==Solution==
Let <imath>x = \text{lcm}(a, b)</imath>, and <imath>y = \text{gcd}(a, b)</imath>. Therefore, <imath>a\cdot b = \text{lcm}(a, b)\cdot \text{gcd}(a, b) = x\cdot y</imath>. Thus, the equation becomes

<cmath>x\cdot y + 63 = 20x + 12y</cmath>
<cmath>x\cdot y - 20x - 12y + 63 = 0</cmath>

Using [[Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick]], we rewrite this equation as

<cmath>(x - 12)(y - 20) - 240 + 63 = 0</cmath>
<cmath>(x - 12)(y - 20) = 177</cmath>

Since <imath>177 = 3\cdot 59</imath> and <imath>x >= y</imath>, we have <imath>x  - 12 = 59</imath> and <imath>y - 20 = 3</imath>, or <imath>x - 12 = 177</imath> and <imath>y - 20 = 1</imath>. This gives us the solutions <imath>(71, 23)</imath> and <imath>(189, 21)</imath>. Since the <imath>\text{GCD}</imath> must be a divisor of the <imath>\text{LCM}</imath>, the first pair does not work. Assume <imath>a>b</imath>. We must have <imath>a = 21 \cdot 9</imath> and <imath>b = 21</imath>, and we could then have <imath>a<b</imath>, so there are <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B)} ~2}</imath> solutions.
